metadata.title: The Legal Briefing Isn't a News Digest.
metadata.purpose: Take the 'legal briefing' skill apart in the Teardown register — explain the machinery (a skill is a folder Claude reads; SKILL.md is the whole program; linear pipeline; exactly three modes), name what the design optimized for and what it sacrificed (predictability inside a small fence, at the cost of anything outside it), and land the verdict: this is a scan of your own email, calendar, and contracts, not outside news.
metadata.anchor_pair: N/A — source is skill-teardown format (anatomy -> pipeline -> constraint -> verdict), no anchor structure to preserve

beats.narration_text: Here's the naive frame: a legal briefing means outside news, delivered each morning. That's not what this is. It's a scan of your own email, calendar, and contracts, organized around what's actually happening in your work. They optimized for the thing you can act on — your own inbox, your own calendar, your open contracts — at the expense of the wider industry ticker you'd get from a headline feed.

beats.act: 1 anatomy — a skill is a folder
beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. The briefing is built from a skill, which is a folder — Claude reads it before it does anything. Inside is one file, written in plain English, that spells out exactly what counts as a briefing here. Claude reads the file, then follows it. The file is the whole program. That's the design choice: no code, no config, no runtime — just prose the model honors. What that buys you is the ability to change the behavior by editing a paragraph. What it costs is any guarantee the model reads it the way you meant.

shot.new_visual_element: A folder icon opening to reveal SKILL.md, references/, scripts/; SKILL.md highlighted

production_viz.label: A skill is a folder
production_viz.mechanic: A folder opens on cream to reveal three items: SKILL.md (highlighted in crimson), a references/ folder, a scripts/ folder. A caption below reads 'Claude reads it, then follows it.'

beats.narration_text: The pipeline is linear. Read the file, work through each step in the order written, return the result. Nothing runs out of sequence unless a step itself says so. That's the whole mechanism. They chose linearity over branching: it's easy to audit and easy to predict, at the cost of being unable to react partway through if the input changes shape.

shot.new_visual_element: Three-phase pipeline: Read SKILL.md -> Execute steps in order -> Return result

production_viz.label: Input in, output out
production_viz.mechanic: Three cards left to right joined by arrows: 'Read SKILL.md', 'Execute steps in order', 'Return result'. Linear, no branch points drawn.

beats.narration_text: Here's the constraint that defines this skill. It covers exactly three situations: a daily scan of legal-relevant items across your email, calendar, and contracts; research on one legal question against your own internal sources; and rapid context when something breaks fast — a breach, a litigation threat, a regulatory inquiry. Ask it anything outside those three and no mode covers it. That's the trade-off they took on purpose. They optimized for reliability inside the fence at the expense of usefulness beyond it. The behavior is predictable because the boundary is small, not because the model is smart.

shot.new_visual_element: Three mode cards: daily scan, topic research, incident response; a boundary line with 'nothing outside this list' beyond it

production_viz.label: Exactly three modes
production_viz.mechanic: Three rows fill in one at a time with a checkmark: 'Daily scan — email, calendar, contracts', 'Topic research — one question, your own sources', 'Incident response — breach, threat, inquiry'. A dashed boundary line beneath the list, with a faint unlabelled field beyond it captioned 'nothing outside this list'.

beats.narration_text: Here's the carry-out. A legal briefing here isn't outside news — it's a scan of what's already in your own email, calendar, and contracts, run through whichever of three fixed modes the moment calls for. It works if you value acting on your own sources; it fails if you need coverage of the wider legal world.

props.quote: A legal briefing here isn't outside news — it's a scan of what's already in your own email, calendar, and contracts, run through whichever of three fixed modes the moment calls for.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt — paste it into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I want a personal legal briefing built from my own sources — my recent email, my next two weeks of calendar, and any contracts I have open. Design the spec: list the items you'd flag as legal-relevant and why, group them into three tiers of urgency, and for each item name the exact follow-up ask if I want a deeper read. Assume I'm not a lawyer and I want fifteen minutes on this a week. Go deeper: which items would you actually escalate to a real lawyer today, and what's the trigger you're waiting for on the rest? Liam, in for Bear.
